**Ephemeral** means lasting for a very short time — fleeting, temporary.

- **Why it matters:** The word often carries a poetic weight — it reminds us that beautiful things (a sunset, a moment of peace) are brief, which is part of what makes them precious.

**Why it matters:** The word pops up in tech a lot (ephemeral messages that auto-delete, ephemeral cloud servers that spin down when you're done) because not everything needs to be permanent.

The **Eiffel Tower** is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in **Paris, France**. It was built by Gustave Eiffel's company for the 1889 World's Fair and was originally meant to be temporary (it was nearly torn down in 1909, but was saved because it made a handy radio antenna).

Standing **330 meters** (1,083 ft) tall, it was the world's tallest structure until the Chrysler Building in 1930. Today it's one of the most recognizable landmarks on the planet and France's most-visited paid monument — roughly 7 million people go up it each year.

The **Eiffel Tower** is a wrought-iron lattice tower in Paris, built by Gustave Eiffel's company for the 1889 World's Fair. It stands 330 m tall (about 1,083 ft), was the world's tallest structure until 1930, and was originally meant to be temporary — it was nearly torn down in 1909 but was saved because its height made it useful for radio antennas. Today it's the most visited paid monument in the world and basically *the* symbol of Paris.

The **Eiffel Tower** is a wrought-iron **lattice tower** on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France — probably the most famous landmark in the world. It was designed by engineer **Gustave Eiffel**, whose company built it for the **1889 World's Fair** (the Exposition Universelle), taking just over two years to complete. 

It's 330 meters (1,083 ft) tall, was the world's tallest structure until the Chrysler Building in 1930, and draws nearly **7 million visitors a year**. Originally criticized by some Parisian artists and intellectuals (who called it an eyesore), it was intended to be temporary — but it survived because it proved useful as a radiotelegraph station. Now it's basically the universal symbol of Paris and France.

**Meticulous** means showing very careful, precise attention to every detail. If you're meticulous, you don't miss the small stuff — you double-check, you're thorough, you dot every *i* and cross every *t*.

**Analogy:** Think of someone packing for a trip who checks the forecast, lays out outfits, rolls everything to save space, counts socks, and still zips the suitcase with a checklist in hand. That's meticulous.

**Why it matters:** Being meticulous is a huge asset in fields like surgery, coding, accounting, or proofreading — where missing one small detail can cause big problems. On the flip side, it can tip into being too slow or anxious about mistakes (the older meaning of the word was "timid" or "fearful").
